parameters.name: id
parameters.description: API token id (`atok_…`) — not the token itself.

resource_id.description: Prefixed id of the affected resource, when there is one.

metadata.description: Action-specific detail; shape varies by action.

actor_kind.description: `staff` means Elaichi support did it: either directly (a `staff.*` action, `actor_user_id` is the staff user, not a member) or while impersonating a member (`actor` is the member and `metadata.impersonated_by_user_id` is the staff user).

actor.description: The person behind this row, named server-side in one batch per page. Read this rather than resolving `actor_user_id` against the member directory: that directory is paginated, so a client resolving ids itself only names the actors on the page it happened to fetch.

name.description: Null (with `email`) when the id is no longer resolvable in this organization — a departed member, which clients render as "Former member".

avatar_url.description: The person's picture — the same one the console's user menu draws: their stored profile picture, else a Gravatar URL (`d=404`, 96px) derived server-side from their email (the address itself is not sent), else null. Draw initials when it is null or the image fails to load.

kind.description: Mirrors `actor_kind`, so a non-human actor stays distinguishable from an unnamed one.

tool_call.description: A connected-tool call (`assistant.toolbox_tool`, `assistant.toolbox.execute`) or synthetic-tool run (`synthetic_tool.executed`) in words, resolved server-side in one batch per source per page; null on every other row. Names are resolved at read time, so renaming or deleting a connection or client changes how old rows read.

summary.description: Outcome-aware sentence, e.g. "Updated a page in Notion" or "Failed to update a page in Notion".

tool_name.description: The catalog tool name, unqualified, when recorded; else the advertised name.

connector.description: Null when no single connector applies (a synthetic tool) or none was recorded or resolvable.

can_view.description: Whether the caller may open this connector (`GET /connector/{slug}`): holds `connector:view` and the catalog resolved the slug. False on the staff feed.

toolbox.description: The stored toolbox the call went through. Null for the built-in all-tools and per-connection sets, for a synthetic-tool row, and for a row that never recorded one.

name.description: Null when the toolbox is gone or the lookup failed.

can_view.description: Whether the caller may open it (`GET /toolbox/{id}`): owner or a grant. False on the staff feed.

synthetic_tool.description: The synthetic tool the call ran: a `synthetic_tool.executed` row, or a toolbox call whose tool was a synthetic one. Null for every ordinary connector-tool call.

name.description: The name it had when it ran.

can_view.description: Whether the caller may open it (`GET /synthetic-tool/{id}`): its owner only. False on the staff feed.

state.description: `unknown` means the lookup failed — never read it as deleted.

can_view.description: Whether the caller may open this connection (`GET /connection/{id}`).

surface.description: `app` the agent window, `console` a person in the console itself (WebMCP, a synthetic tool's Run), `mcp` an MCP client, `api` an org API token. Null when not recorded — never guessed.

client_name.description: The verified client name when its redirect URIs prove it, else the self-reported name.

client_mark.description: The verified client's bundled-mark slug; set only when `client_verified` is true.

client_verified.description: True only when the name and logo come from the verified client.

error_message.description: Fixed plain-English sentence for `error`; null on success.

approval.description: `direct_run`: a person ran a synthetic tool directly (console Run or `POST /synthetic-tool/{id}/execute`), so no gate asked — not the same as `not_required` (a read). On `assistant.toolbox.execute` the requirement follows the tool's own tier. Null when the row predates the recorded facts, or the source is not one of these.

target.description: What the call touched. A list, search or query has the type alone (id, name, url null). Null when nothing could be identified. On the staff feed name and url are always null, here and in `metadata.target`.

id.description: The path id or the created record's id. Never an email address.

name.description: The object's title. Always null for a person's record (by resource noun or by response shape), for a message-like record (email, thread, comment, event, post, ...), and when it contains an email address.

url.description: http(s), no user:password, origin + path only (query and fragment dropped). Null for a create-like call and for any call whose resource or method names a session, signed/temporary/download link, export, portal, checkout, invite or recipient view.

result_count.description: Items a list, search or query returned.

get.description: Append-only trail of what happened in this organization, newest first. Open to every member: with `audit:view` it lists every event in the organization; without it, only the caller's own events plus events on connections they own or can edit. The response says which, as a top-level `scope` (`org` or `own`) beside the list envelope. An `own` response also carries `connection_scope`: `all`, `one` (a `connection_id` was given), or `too_many` — the caller owns or can edit more connections than one query lists, so the page holds only their own events. Anyone who can edit a connection (owner, or an `edit` grant direct, through a team, or org-wide) sees every member's tool calls made through it. Filters combine with AND; `q` additionally matches the actor by name or email. The cursor is opaque — do not parse or construct one. Events are eventually consistent: one may take a moment to appear after the action that produced it.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Matches the action, the resource, or the actor by name/email. `system` matches system-generated rows. LIKE wildcards are matched literally. Max 200 characters.

parameters.name: category
parameters.description: Bucket derived from the action name. Any other value is a 400.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: Verb class of the action, not the full action name.

parameters.name: actor
parameters.description: A user id (`usr_…`), or the literal `system` for rows with no human actor. Max 128 characters.

parameters.name: connection_id
parameters.description: Only events on this connection (`conn_…`). Needs `audit:view`, or owning the connection, or `edit` on it; otherwise 404, the same as an id that does not exist. Max 128 characters.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Inclusive lower bound on `created_at`. ISO-8601; anything unparseable is a 400.

slug.description: Stable connector key — this is the identifier everywhere, not an id.

owner.description: Catalog owner. Org-owned values mark this org's custom connectors. Always this string — the owning MEMBER is `owner_member`, a separate field, so a client never has to tell a string from an object.

avatar_url.description: The person's picture — the same one the console's user menu draws: their stored profile picture, else a Gravatar URL (`d=404`, 96px) derived server-side from their email (the address itself is not sent), else null. Draw initials when it is null or the image fails to load.

owner_member.description: The resolved owning member, the same shape as a toolbox's `owner`. Org-owned rows the caller reaches (ownership or a grant) only: an object when somebody OTHER than the caller owns the connector (just `{ id }` for an owner who has left the org); `null` when the connector has no owner yet (an ownerless connector — see `POST /connector/{slug}/owner`); absent when the caller owns it (`owner_user_id` already says so) or reaches it by nothing but `connector:view`. Names come from one batched lookup per page.

custom.description: True for a connector this organization authored or forked.

kind.description: `remote_mcp` for an organization's own bring-your-own remote MCP connector (its tools are discovered per connection, not read from the catalog), `catalog` for every other connector. Read it instead of guessing from the slug. On the detail, a remote MCP connector also carries `remote_mcp` (`url`, `auth_mode`, `oauth_registration`, `catalog_owner`, `listed_tool_count` — the server's count of the rows `GET /connector/{slug}/tool` lists to this caller with no filter, turned-off tools included for a caller who can manage the connector — and `support_contact`, the email or https link staff entered for a connector Elaichi publishes, null otherwise) and `auth`; its `tool_count` is the server's count of the tools that are switched on.

byoa.description: True when the connector needs a customer OAuth app (BYOA) — a placeholder client id, a real id with a placeholder secret, or a real id with no platform OAuth secret stored for it. The first two are derived from the config on the catalog summary, so they are on every row; the third comes from one cached platform-credential read.

single_redirect_auth.description: A hint, not a promise: true when connecting this connector is most likely a provider sign-in with nothing to fill in first — exactly one auth method, and that method can redirect (OAuth). A list row judges the auth methods only; `GET /connector/{slug}` also rules out a method with form fields or a `permissions_text` notice. A client may use it to get a popup window ready inside the click that starts a connect. `direct_connect_url` on the `POST /connection` / reconnect response stays authoritative.

can_fork.description: Whether THIS caller may fork the connector, computed server-side so a client never re-derives it: false for a remote MCP connector (`POST /connector/{slug}/fork` answers `409 connector_not_forkable`), for a connector the caller is restricted from, without `connector:create`, and when the plan does not include custom connectors. On `GET /connector` rows and `GET /connector/{slug}`.

owner_user_id.description: Owning member (`usr_…`), from the connector's `connector_owner` row. Present only on an org-owned row the caller reaches (ownership or a grant) AND that has an owner — an ownerless connector has none until `POST /connector/{slug}/owner` (or the creator backfill) assigns one, and a member browsing on `connector:view` alone is not told whose it is — such a connector is not shown to them at all (org owners/admins included). The owner is implicit `edit`, plus delete and transfer — the two things no share confers.

can_use.description: Whether the caller may create (or re-authenticate) a connection from this connector — the `use` floor `POST /connection` and `POST /connection/{id}/reconnect` enforce, which answers 403 `connector_not_shared` when it is not met. For an org-owned connector: ownership or a `use`-or-better grant (direct, team or org-wide). Always true on a platform catalog row, which has no ACL. This is the SHARING answer, independent of `restricted`: a connector shared for viewing only is listed but not connectable, and a client should leave Connect off rather than show a button that refuses. A connector nobody shared with the caller at all is not listed.

can_manage.description: Present only on org-owned/custom connector rows (omitted for platform catalog rows, which have no ACL concept). Whether the caller may edit this connector's config — ownership or a real `edit` grant of their own. `connector:manage` alone no longer implies this (removed 2026-09-04): org owners/admins do not manage-by-default a connector nobody explicitly shared with them.

can_transfer.description: Org-owned rows only. Whether the caller may transfer this connector — ownership, full stop; no `connector:manage` fallback. Mirrors `POST /connector/{slug}/transfer`. False for everyone on an ownerless connector (transfer needs an owner). Not the delete gate — see `can_delete`.

can_delete.description: Org-owned rows only. Whether the caller may delete this connector: the owner, and only the owner, so false for everyone on an ownerless connector. Currently the same formula as `can_transfer`, kept as its own field so a client gates Delete on the delete question. Mirrors `DELETE /connector/{slug}`; the console gates its Delete on this.

can_assign_owner.description: Org-owned rows only. Whether the caller may give this ownerless connector an owner: it has no owner row AND the caller holds `connector:manage`. Mirrors `POST /connector/{slug}/owner` naming another member. Independent of the caller's reach, so a manager browsing the catalog can see that a connector needs an owner; it says nothing about who has access.

can_claim.description: Org-owned rows only. Whether the caller may make THEMSELVES the owner: `can_assign_owner` AND a real `edit` grant of their own. `connector:manage` alone never makes its holder the owner of a connector nobody shared with them. Mirrors `POST /connector/{slug}/owner` naming the caller.

can_revoke_share.description: Org-owned rows only. `can_share`'s formula — edit access or ownership AND `connector:share` — a THIRD formula, distinct from `can_manage`: an `edit` grantee whose role omits `connector:share` can reconfigure the connector but was never meant to grant or revoke someone else's access. Mirrors `DELETE /connector/{slug}/share/{aclId}`.

restricted.description: True when the caller's restrictions block this whole connector. A blocked connector is LISTED and flagged, never omitted — a picker that only got "no match" could not tell "your admin blocked it" from "that provider does not exist". It still cannot be connected: `POST /connection` and `GET /connector/{slug}/tools` refuse it.

restricted_by.description: Which precedence layer the winning rule came from, or null when nothing blocks this connector. Adds *which* to `restricted`'s *whether* and nothing else — no rule id, author, reason or coverage. Same field and same meaning as on `GET /connector/{slug}` and on a connection row.

slug.description: The upstream connector the restriction is inherited from. For API consumers; never render it. Null — together with `label` — when the caller may not be told the upstream (an org-owned upstream they hold no grant on, or one that was deleted): a slug names the connector as surely as its label does.

label.description: The upstream's display name — null, together with `slug`, when the caller may not be told it. The UI then says "a connector this was forked from".

restricted_inherited_from.description: Set when this connector is restricted for the caller ONLY because the connector it was forked from is — a fork inherits its upstream's restrictions on purpose (forking a blocked connector is not a bypass), but nothing was set on the fork itself, so this says where the block came from. Null when not restricted, when a rule names this connector directly, or when the lineage could not be walked. Asking for access still targets THIS connector: approving the fork's own request lifts the inherited block for that fork only. Sibling of `restricted_by` (which stays the precedence layer); computed server-side in the same batch as the restriction evaluation — clients must not derive it from lineage.

access_via.description: How the CALLER reaches this connector — not who else can. `owner` — they own it. `direct` — a grant naming them personally. `team` — a grant to a team they belong to (or, per §6.2, one they administer), named in `access_via_team`. `org` — an organization-wide grant. When several sources apply the BROADEST wins and the caller's access level is not consulted: owner, else `org`, else `team`, else `direct`. So a caller granted `edit` personally AND `view` org-wide reads `org` — a narrower grant must never mask org-wide exposure, since this field says how far the connector reaches, not what the caller may do with it. Deliberately NOT gated on `can_see_shares`, and deliberately not a widening of it: this is the caller's OWN grant and their OWN team memberships, so a `view`/`use` grantee receives it while the grantee list — information about colleagues — stays closed to them. No other member is ever named. ABSENT when nothing reaches the caller — a transfer answering the ex-owner of a resource that was never shared, or a catalog row browsed with no grant behind it. Absent means "no source to name", never "not permitted", and never an implied `org`.

access_via_team.description: Present exactly when `access_via` is `team`, absent otherwise. The team the caller reaches this connector through — one of their own teams, never a disclosure about anybody else.

name.description: Team display name, or null when the team no longer resolves in the directory — the same null contract every resolved grantee name carries.

get.description: The platform catalog — visible to every role, `connector:view` included — plus this organization's own custom connectors, listed ONLY for their owner and the members a grant reaches, like connections and toolboxes: a custom connector nobody shared with the caller is absent (and `404` by slug), whatever their role — `connector:view` and `connector:manage` widen nothing, an org admin included. The filter runs inside a fill loop, so a page holds `limit` rows whenever the caller can see that many, and `next_cursor` is set only when a visible row follows (one exception: a request that examines more than 4000 consecutive hidden connectors matching one query without finding a visible one returns an empty page with a cursor so paging can continue); it is sealed (opaque), bound to the organization and to the `search`/`category`/`custom` query it was returned for, and a cursor that does not open or is replayed under another query is a `400`. A search matching only hidden connectors is otherwise an empty page with a null cursor, exactly like a search matching nothing. There is no `?visibility=org` oversight mode (removed 2026-09-04); `can_manage` on an org-owned row reflects only a real `edit` grant of their own. Platform catalog rows omit `can_manage` (no ACL concept) and carry `can_use: true`. Connectors the caller's restrictions block are RETURNED, flagged `restricted`/`restricted_by`, not filtered out — a restriction flags, a missing grant hides. `prev_cursor` is always null here.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Substring match on the connector name/label.

parameters.name: custom
parameters.description: Send `true` to narrow to this organization's own connectors.

post.description: Authors a new org-owned connector, either from a catalog `config` or — bring your own — from a remote streamable-HTTP MCP server (`remote_mcp`). Send exactly one of the two. Requires `connector:create` and the `custom_connectors` plan feature. The config is schema-validated: a malformed one answers 422 with the exact issues. The slug is permanent and must be unique within the catalog. A remote MCP connector is private to its creator until shared (the ordinary connector grants), and its tools are discovered per connection, not at creation. `remote_mcp.url` must be https, must not name Elaichi itself, and is immutable afterwards. `auth_mode` says how members sign in: `oauth_auto` (Elaichi registers itself with the server's authorization server — Client ID Metadata Document first, else dynamic registration; 400 when neither exists), `oauth_client` (your own `client_id` and optional `client_secret`), `custom` (an `auth_config` declaring a token form, no OAuth) or `none`. Absent, it is inferred: `client_id` means `oauth_client`, `auth_config` means `custom`, and otherwise the server is probed (OAuth metadata means `oauth_auto`, even when it also answers anonymously; a server with no sign-in at all answers 400 `sign_in_not_offered` unless you send `auth_mode: "none"`; anything else answers 400 `remote_mcp_auth_required`). A field that does not belong to the mode is a 400. The OAuth client is stored as the organization's own app for the connector, never in the connector entry. An organization may hold 25 remote MCP connectors (409 `remote_mcp_server_limit`). The 201 is the connector detail, with `kind: "remote_mcp"`, `remote_mcp` (`url`, `auth_mode`, `oauth_registration`) and `auth` (what sign-in the connector declares, names only — never a secret).

auth_config.description: `custom` only: `credentials` (an `api_key` form), `authorization`, `headers`, `query` — the shape of a connector config minus `resources`. Values are placeholders (`{{api_key}}`); a literal secret is refused.

scopes.description: OAuth only. Defaults to what the server advertises.

omit_refresh_scope.description: OAuth modes only (400 for `custom` and `none`). Off by default. `true` makes a token refresh send no `scope` (RFC 6749 §6: omitted means the original grant); the RFC 8707 `resource` is still sent. For a server that rejects a scope on refresh, such as Close (`400 invalid_scope`). Echoed as `auth.omit_refresh_scope`.

logo.description: `remote_mcp` only. An https URL.

slug.description: Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. `new` is reserved.

config.description: Connector definition (resources, methods, auth). Mutually exclusive with `remote_mcp`; `config.remote_mcp` is reserved.

get.description: Every category value used across the catalog this organization can see — the platform catalog plus its own custom connectors — from a full scan, not just whatever page `GET /connector` happens to have returned so far. Use this to populate a category filter; use `GET /connector?category=` to apply one. Briefly cached server-side, so a category added or removed by a custom-connector edit can take a short while to show up here. Requires `connector:view`.

kind.description: `remote_mcp` for an organization's own remote MCP connector (`POST /connector` with `remote_mcp`, whose detail also carries `remote_mcp` and `auth`), `catalog` for every other connector. Read it instead of guessing from the slug.

single_redirect_auth.description: Hint: exactly one auth method, it can redirect (OAuth), and it has no form fields and no `permissions_text`. `direct_connect_url` on the connect response stays authoritative.

tool_count.description: The provider's total. For a remote MCP connector Elaichi publishes, the organization's switched-on tools once anyone in it has connected, and until then the length of the tool list staff published for it (never 0 for a server that publishes tools).

connect_notes.description: Remote MCP connectors only: markdown a person should read BEFORE connecting (an admin setting to turn on first, the plan it bills, which region or site to pick). The same text the sign-in page shows above its Connect button (the OAuth config's `permissions_text`). Render it as sanitized markdown. Null when there is none, and for every catalog connector. Detail only.

connect_notes_link.description: An https guide to that setup (the OAuth config's `documentation_link`). Null when unset.

get.description: Catalog detail plus `restricted`, which reports whether the caller's restrictions block this connector — a restricted connector still resolves here but cannot be connected or executed. For an org-owned connector the response also carries its config, `owner_user_id`/`owner_member`, `can_use`, `can_manage`, `can_share` (mirrors `POST /:slug/share`'s own gate: edit access or ownership AND `connector:share`, never a `connector:manage` fallback), `can_transfer` (ownership only), `can_delete` (owner only), `can_revoke_share`, `can_assign_owner`, `can_claim`, the bounded `access_summary` (same shape as connection/toolbox's — counts plus a few resolved names, the owner excluded; page `GET /:slug/share` for the full grant list) and `shares`, present only when the caller is the owner or has a real `edit` grant of their own — never for a bare `connector:manage` holder with no grant (removed 2026-09-04: org owners/admins do not see access details nobody explicitly shared with them, and there is no oversight audit trail for connectors any more). A custom connector the caller cannot see is `404`, never `403`. Platform catalog connectors need only `connector:view`.

patch.description: **`config` is REPLACED wholesale when present** — send the complete definition, since anything omitted is gone. `label` and `category` are ordinary merge-patch fields. Org-owned connectors only, and the caller needs edit access (ownership or an `edit` share). Existing connections keep working, but tools removed from the config stop resolving in every toolbox that names them. A remote MCP connector (`kind: "remote_mcp"`) takes a different body: `label`, `category`, `logo`, `description`, `auth_config` (`custom` sign-in only; replaces the declaration whole, and the response carries `reconnect_required: true` when its fields changed so existing connections must sign in again), `client_id` / `client_secret` (`oauth_client` only; an omitted secret keeps the stored one) and `omit_refresh_scope` (OAuth only, else 400 `omit_refresh_scope_not_oauth`; `true` sets it, `false` removes it, read at the next token refresh, so no `reconnect_required`) and `connect_notes` / `connect_notes_link` (OAuth only, else 400 `connect_notes_not_oauth`; `null` clears; stored in place in the OAuth config as `permissions_text` / `documentation_link`, so no `reconnect_required`). Its `url` cannot be changed (400: it would send members' tokens to a different host — create a new connector) and neither can its raw `config` (400).

config.description: Replaces the stored config entirely. Refused on a remote MCP connector.

logo.description: Remote MCP connectors only. An https URL.

auth_config.description: Remote MCP connectors with `custom` sign-in only.

client_id.description: Remote MCP connectors with `oauth_client` sign-in only.

omit_refresh_scope.description: Remote MCP connectors with OAuth sign-in only. `true`: a token refresh sends no scope; `false`: back to the default. Members do not need to reconnect.

connect_notes.description: Remote MCP connectors with OAuth sign-in only. Markdown shown before sign-in (trimmed). `null` clears it.

connect_notes_link.description: As `connect_notes`. An https link with no credentials. `null` clears it.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

delete.description: Irreversible. Refused with 409 while any connection still uses this connector — delete or transfer those first — so it cannot strand vaulted accounts or toolbox tools. Org-owned connectors only. Owner only: `edit` may modify a connector but never delete it (docs/access-model.md §2), so an `edit` grantee gets 403, and a connector with no owner row answers 403 with `code: "connector_ownerless"` to an `edit` grantee (a caller without `edit` is refused first) until `POST /connector/{slug}/owner` assigns one. Clears the connector's owner row and grants before it is removed, so a later connector reusing the slug inherits neither.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

post.description: Changes the connector's owner. Every existing grant is left exactly as it was, so nobody who could already reach it loses that reach; the new owner gains only what ownership itself confers (implicit `edit`, plus delete and transfer). The previous owner held no grant row, so they are left at `use` in the same call (unless they already reach `use` or `edit` another way) — otherwise every connection they made through the connector would be blocked as `connector_not_shared` the moment they gave it away. The new owner can revoke that grant like any other; member offboarding is the exception and leaves a departing owner nothing. The target must be an active member of the organization. Allowed for the current owner only — no `connector:manage` fallback, and an ownerless connector has nobody who may transfer it (403; use `POST /connector/{slug}/owner`). A transfer that races another transfer (or the owner's removal from the org, which deletes the owner row) answers 409 rather than taking the connector back. Recorded in the audit log as `connector.transferred`. The 200 is the connector as the CALLER now sees it, so a previous owner (now a `use` grantee) gets no `owner_user_id`, no `shares` and no manage capabilities back. The audit row carries `previous_owner_kept_use`.

owner_user_id.description: New owning member (`usr_…`).

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

post.summary: Assign an owner to an ownerless connector
post.description: Gives a connector that has no owner an owner, and nothing else — every grant is left as it was. Never moves an existing owner: a connector that already has one answers 409 `connector_has_owner` (that is `POST /connector/{slug}/transfer`, owner only), and so does a claim that loses a race with another claim or the creator backfill. Requires `connector:manage`. The target must be an active member of the organization. Naming yourself additionally requires a real `edit` grant of your own (`can_claim`) — a bare `connector:manage` never makes its holder the owner of a connector nobody shared with them (403); naming someone else needs no grant of yours, so a `connector:manage` holder who reaches nothing may assign it. 404 only for a slug that is not an org-owned connector. Recorded in the audit log as `connector.owner_assigned`. The 200 is the connector as the CALLER now sees it.

owner_user_id.description: New owning member (`usr_…`).

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

name.description: Exact tool name — what a toolbox entry's `tool_name` must contain.

input_schema.description: JSON Schema for the tool arguments.

title.description: The upstream server's human title for the tool. Present only on a remote MCP tool that has one.

tier.description: Always present. What the approval gate and the MCP scope ladder treat this tool as — `classifyToolMethod`, the one function they share, so a badge can never disagree with the gate. A remote MCP tool's is derived from the server's annotations (unannotated means `destructive`) and always follows it, up or down, on a refresh. A system-catalog tool whose method documents `mcp_annotations` takes the tier those give (an HTTP DELETE is always `destructive`); any other catalog tool, including every custom connector and fork tool, takes it from its method and HTTP verb. Never infer a remote MCP tool from it: read `kind`.

kind.description: `remote_mcp` for a tool from a remote MCP connector (its `resource` is the constant `mcp`, its `method` the upstream name, and `title` may be set), `catalog` for every other tool.

tier_source.description: Why a remote MCP tool's `tier` is what it is: `server` (the MCP server's own annotations decided it) or `default` (the server labeled the tool neither way, so the MCP safe default `destructive` applies). Lets a client say "Not labeled" rather than show a tier nobody chose. Present only on a remote MCP tool.

restricted.description: True when the caller's restrictions block THIS tool. Blocked tools are returned flagged, never omitted — a shorter list is no signal, because nobody knows the length it should have been. Presence is not permission: execution still refuses it. The connector-level 403 is a separate question and is unchanged.

restricted_by.description: Which precedence layer's rule blocks this tool, null when none does. Same field, union and meaning as on connector and connection rows: adds *which* to `restricted`'s *whether* and nothing else — no rule id, author, reason or coverage. `restricted === (restricted_by !== null)` always.

restricted_scope.description: `"connector"` when the tool is refused because its WHOLE connector is restricted for the caller, `"tool"` for a rule about the tool itself, null exactly when `restricted_by` is. Decides which ask can succeed: a tool request on a connector restricted whole is refused (`409 tool_request_connector_blocked`), so ask for the connector. On this listing it is only ever `"tool"` when set, since a connector restricted whole 403s the route; toolbox entries carry the same field and can say `"connector"`.

operation.description: The CRUD bucket this tool falls into, computed server-side from its resolved HTTP verb (`src/connector/toolOperation.ts`) — never re-derive it client-side. Filter with `?operation=`.

operation_counts.description: How many tools of each CRUD bucket the `q` filter alone leaves — never narrowed further by `operation` itself, so the count beside an unselected filter chip stays honest. Repeated on every page.

get.description: Every tool this connector defines, each flagged `restricted`/`restricted_by` for the caller — the catalog view, with no account behind it. Use it to pick `tool_name` values for toolbox entries. For what one authenticated account can actually run, use `GET /connection/{id}/tools`. Blocked tools are flagged, not omitted; the model-facing `connector.list_tools` operation still omits them, because a tool a model may not call is a wasted turn while a person picking one needs to see why it is unavailable. `q` and `operation` are both applied before paging, and `operation_counts` describes the `q`-filtered set (never narrowed further by `operation` itself), so the console's filter chips stay honest under a search. A restricted connector answers 403. A custom connector the caller cannot see answers 404 (checked before the restriction, so the 403 never confirms it exists). Requires `connector:view`.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring match on `name`, `description` and `resource`. LIKE wildcards are matched literally. Max 200 characters.

parameters.name: operation
parameters.description: Comma-separated CRUD buckets to keep: read, create, update, delete, other. Unknown values 400. Applied before paging, so the cursor never counts a row the filter would have hidden.

get.summary: List a remote MCP connector's tool registry

match_count.description: How many tools match this request's `q` / `tier` / `labeled` (and the caller's `status`), counted on the server. Only on a first page of a narrowed list; absent otherwise.

get.description: The registry the organization keeps for one of its own remote MCP connectors: one row per tool NAME, decided once for every connection of the connector (which of those names a particular connection lists is its own business). A tool the server offers is usable at once. Rows carry `status` (`active`, or `disabled` when a manager turned it off), the `tier` (derived from the server's annotations, always follows the server on a refresh, up or down), `tier_source` (`server`: the server's own annotations decided the tier; `default`: the server sent no `readOnlyHint: true` and no boolean `destructiveHint`, so the tier is MCP's safe default `destructive` and the console draws no access tag for it), the whole `description` of the latest definition (bounded at sync to 8,000 characters), `connection_count` (how many connections list it now) and `can_manage` (the caller may `PATCH` it). A caller with only `use` access sees just the `active` tools, every row reading `active`, whatever `status` they ask for. The detail's `remote_mcp.listed_tool_count` is this list (no filter) counted on the server. Keyset-paged by name; `q` is a case-insensitive substring of the name, upstream name, title or description (a space also matches `_`), `status`, `tier` (one or several) and `labeled` filter, all on the server before paging (so the cursor and an empty page speak for the filtered set). When `q`, `tier` or `labeled` narrows the list, the first page (no `cursor`) also carries `match_count`: the server's count of every tool matching those same filters, to read beside `listed_tool_count` as "N of M tools" instead of counting the pages held. Needs `use` access or better on the connector (a `view` grant answers 403, no reach at all answers 404, a connector with no remote MCP server answers 404) and the `custom_connectors` plan feature. Not `GET /connector/{slug}/tools`, which is the catalog capability listing.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned remote MCP connector.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Substring of the name, upstream name, title or description. LIKE wildcards are matched literally. Max 200 characters.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Only tools that are on (`active`) or off (`disabled`). Managers only; a `use` grantee always gets `active`.

parameters.name: tier
parameters.description: Only tools whose stored tier is this one, or any of several: a comma list (`tier=read,write`) or the parameter repeated. It is the tier the gate enforces, so `tier=destructive` includes the tools the server left unlabeled (`tier_source: "default"`). Pair with `labeled=true` for server labels only. Empty is no filter; any value that is not `read`, `write` or `destructive` is a 400.

parameters.name: labeled
parameters.description: `true`: only tools the server labeled itself (`tier_source: "server"`); `false`: only the ones it left unlabeled. Empty is no filter; any other value is a 400.

patch.summary: Turn a remote MCP connector tool off or on
patch.description: `status: "disabled"` switches the tool off for every connection, `"active"` turns it back on; nothing else is accepted (400). A tool's tier is always the server's label and cannot be set here. Needs the connector's own edit access (ownership or an `edit` share) on an org's own connector, `connector:manage` on one Elaichi publishes. The 200 is the tool with its whole definition (`description`, `input_schema`, `output_schema`, `annotations`, `derived_tier`). Recorded in the audit log as `connector.tool_updated` with the status before and after.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of a remote MCP connector.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The tool's Elaichi name, as `GET /connector/{slug}/tool` returns it.

post.summary: Fork connector into an org-owned copy
post.description: Copies a catalog connector into this organization under a new slug, tracking the original as upstream so later changes can be pulled. Forking a connector the caller's restrictions block is refused — otherwise a fork would launder it under a slug no restriction names. A remote MCP connector (`kind: 'remote_mcp'`) cannot be forked: `409 connector_not_forkable`. Requires `connector:create`.

get.summary: Preview upstream changes for a forked connector
get.description: Read-only diff against the upstream connector, returning individually selectable change ids for `POST /connector/{slug}/pull`. A fork with no upstream answers 400 — link one first with `POST /connector/{slug}/link-upstream`.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned fork.

post.description: Applies exactly the changes whose ids you list, from the preview — nothing else is touched. Re-run the preview first: ids are computed from the current diff and go stale.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned fork.

post.description: Points an older fork at an upstream connector so it can use the pull workflow. New forks are linked automatically; re-linking an already-linked connector answers 409.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned fork.

delete.description: Removes the connector's declared upstream link. Needs `connector:manage`, not merely edit on the connector: a restriction on an upstream also binds everything declared downstream of it, so detaching that link would otherwise let a fork's own author shed a block while keeping the connector's live connections. Use it to repair a lineage row pointed at the wrong upstream; `POST` the correct one afterwards.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

put.description: Documentation is what turns a connector method into a tool: an item with an empty `description` UN-documents that method, and an undocumented method is not offered as a tool. Items must reference methods that exist in the config. An item with neither `resource` nor `method` sets the connector-level description. Sent items are upserted; methods you do not mention are left as they are.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

get.summary: Read this org’s OAuth application for a connector

oauth_app_mode.description: Which application connects on this connector use.

has_client_secret.description: Whether a secret is stored. The secret itself is never returned.

scope.description: Scope overrides this org stored, or null when it kept the catalog scopes.

user_scope.description: Space-separated authorize-URL scopes (`params.user_scope`), or null. Null also when one is stored but held back, see `user_scope_masked`.

user_scope_masked.description: True when a `user_scope` is stored encrypted by an older write and cannot be read or changed here. A `PUT` that sets `user_scope` then answers `409`.

supports_user_scope.description: Whether this connector’s provider takes user token scopes (Slack does). Where false, a `user_scope` that differs from the stored one is refused with `400`.

get.description: Whether connects on this connector use Elaichi’s platform application or one this organization supplied, and the client id if so. The client secret is never returned — `has_client_secret` reports only whether one is stored. Answers `404` for a connector this organization owns (edit its credentials with `PATCH /connector/{slug}` instead — the message says so only to a caller who can see it) and, for every other connector, unless the connector needs a customer OAuth application (`byoa: true` on `GET /connector/{slug}`) OR this organization already has one stored (`oauth_app_mode: "byoa"`) for it — a stored override stays reachable even after the catalog stops requiring one. oauth_app_mode.description: Which application connects on this connector use.

has_client_secret.description: Whether a secret is stored. The secret itself is never returned.

scope.description: Scope overrides this org stored, or null when it kept the catalog scopes.

user_scope.description: Space-separated authorize-URL scopes (`params.user_scope`), or null. Null also when one is stored but held back, see `user_scope_masked`.

user_scope_masked.description: True when a `user_scope` is stored encrypted by an older write and cannot be read or changed here. A `PUT` that sets `user_scope` then answers `409`.

409.description: The stored `user_scope` is held encrypted by an older write and cannot be changed here (`user_scope_masked`). Remove the OAuth application and add it again to replace it.

put.description: Replaces the stored application wholesale, with one exception the setup form depends on: omitting `client_secret` keeps the secret already stored, so correcting a typo in the client id cannot destroy a working secret. client_secret.description: Omit to keep the stored secret. Never returned by any endpoint.

scope.description: Omit to keep the catalog scopes; an array overrides them wholesale.

user_scope.description: Authorize-URL scopes (`params.user_scope`), separated by spaces or commas and stored space-separated. Only where `supports_user_scope` is true; omit to clear.

delete.description: Removes the override so later connects fall back to Elaichi’s platform application. Existing connections made through the removed application are not revoked. Requires `connector:manage`.

get.description: Cursor-paginated, the same shape as `GET /connection/{id}/share` and `GET /toolbox/{id}/share` — a connector may be shared with every member of the organization, so nothing embeds the grant list unbounded. parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Match member name or email, or team name. LIKE wildcards are matched literally. Max 200 characters.

parameters.name: grantee_type
parameters.description: Restrict to one kind of grantee.

post.description: Grants a user, team, or the whole org access to an org-owned connector at a level — the same `view` < `use` < `edit` ladder every shareable resource uses (docs/access-model.md §3): `use` here means creating connections from this connector, `edit` additionally means changing its config and its own grants. parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Connector slug of an org-owned connector.

delete.description: The grantee loses access immediately. Connections already created on the connector keep working.

parameters.name: aclId
parameters.description: ACL entry id from the share list.

slug.description: The upstream connector the restriction is inherited from. For API consumers; never render it. label.description: The upstream's display name — null, together with `slug`, when the caller may not be told it. The UI then says "a connector this was forked from".

Null when not restricted, when a rule names this connector directly, or when the lineage could not be walked. connector_slug.description: Which connector this account is on.

owner_user_id.description: Owning member (`usr_…`); calls run as this identity. Owner is implicit `edit`, plus delete and transfer — the two things no share confers. label.description: Catalog display name; the slug itself when the catalog cannot resolve it.

logo.description: Logo URL; null when the connector has none.

upstream_slug.description: Present only on a fork (an org-owned connector with a lineage): the connector it was forked from. Omitted when the caller has no reach on the fork or on a private upstream (naming it would disclose its slug), and when the lineage cannot be read.

single_redirect_auth.description: The connector-row hint of the same name: connecting is most likely a single provider sign-in, so a client reserves a popup inside the Reconnect click. available.description: False only when the catalog positively does not have the connector (staff unpublished or deleted a platform connector): the connection is kept but nothing can work until it returns. On `GET /connection/{id}` it is `true` when the connector resolves; on a `GET /connection` row it is never `true`, only `false` or ABSENT (one batched lookup per page). auth_mode.description: `GET /connection/{id}` only, remote MCP connectors only, and only when `can_view_connector`: how the connector signs in, so a screen can say "No sign-in" instead of "API key".

can_view_connector.description: `GET /connection/{id}` only. Whether `GET /connector/{slug}` would answer this caller: false for a connector the catalog no longer resolves, without `connector:view`, and for an org-owned connector nobody shared with them (it 404s). Link to the connector only when true.

saffron_account_id.description: Vault account holding the credential. Null until the connect flow completes.

status.description: `pending` = created but not yet authenticated (open `connect_url`); `active` = usable; `needs_reauth` = the credential expired or was revoked upstream, call reconnect; `disconnected` = no longer usable. Refreshed lazily against the vault when connections are read.

access.description: The caller's relationship to this connection: `owner`, or a granted `view`/`use`/`edit` level. There is no oversight fallback for connections — this is never `"oversight"`; a connection the caller neither owns nor holds a grant on is not visible to them at all, whatever organization permission they hold.

owner.description: Who `owner_user_id` is, resolved server-side in the same batch as `connected_by_label` (one per page). Same audience as a toolbox's `owner`: present on a connection the caller does NOT own, absent on their own. On every branch that returns a connection — list, detail and the command responses, so a transfer names the new owner without a reload. `name`/`email` are absent for an owner who has left the organization ("Former member").

name.description: Display name, else the email.

avatar_url.description: The person's picture — the same one the console's user menu draws: their stored profile picture, else a Gravatar URL (`d=404`, 96px) derived server-side from their email (the address itself is not sent), else null. Draw initials when it is null or the image fails to load.

shares.description: Present only when the caller may see the ACL: owner or `edit` access. A `view`/`use` recipient is never told who else the connection is shared with. Absent (not empty) when the caller may not see it.

can_share.description: Whether the caller may share this connection — owner, `edit` access, or a team admin on a team-granted one. No `connection:manage` fallback. Computed server-side (CLAUDE.md's API-first rule); the console reads this rather than re-deriving it from `owner_user_id`/permissions.

can_transfer.description: Present on every list and detail row. Whether the caller may transfer or delete this connection — owner, full stop. No `connection:manage` fallback. total.description: Every grant, the org-wide one included.

preview.description: At most 5 grantees, broadest first (org, then teams, then members), for a hover preview.

name.description: Display name; null for org grants and for grantees no longer in the org.

access_summary.description: Present only when `can_share` is true. Bounded by design — page `GET /connection/{id}/share` for the grants themselves.

name.description: Team display name, or null when the team no longer resolves in the directory — the same null contract every resolved grantee name carries.

get.description: Exactly docs/access-model.md §4, always — connections the caller owns, plus every connection shared with them directly, through a team they belong to, or org-wide. upstream_slug.description: Present only on a fork (an org-owned connector with a lineage): the connector it was forked from. Omitted when the caller has no reach on the fork or on a private upstream (naming it would disclose its slug), and when the lineage cannot be read.

single_redirect_auth.description: The connector-row hint of the same name: connecting is most likely a single provider sign-in, so a client reserves a popup inside the Reconnect click. Always stated on `GET /connection/{id}` (false when `can_view_connector` is). On a list row it is stated only where the caller could open the connector, and ABSENT otherwise, which reads as unknown, never false.

available.description: False only when the catalog positively does not have the connector (staff unpublished or deleted a platform connector): the connection is kept but nothing can work until it returns. On `GET /connection/{id}` it is `true` when the connector resolves; on a `GET /connection` row it is never `true`, only `false` or ABSENT (one batched lookup per page). ABSENT too when the catalog could not answer, so a blip never reads as an unpublished connector.

auth_mode.description: `GET /connection/{id}` only, remote MCP connectors only, and only when `can_view_connector`: how the connector signs in, so a screen can say "No sign-in" instead of "API key".

can_view_connector.description: `GET /connection/{id}` only. Whether `GET /connector/{slug}` would answer this caller: false for a connector the catalog no longer resolves, without `connector:view`, and for an org-owned connector nobody shared with them (it 404s). Link to the connector only when true.

saffron_account_id.description: Vault account holding the credential. Null until the connect flow completes.

status.description: `pending` = created but not yet authenticated (open `connect_url`); `active` = usable; `needs_reauth` = the credential expired or was revoked upstream, call reconnect; `disconnected` = no longer usable. Refreshed lazily against the vault when connections are read.

access.description: The caller's relationship to this connection: `owner`, or a granted `view`/`use`/`edit` level. There is no oversight fallback for connections — this is never `"oversight"`; a connection the caller neither owns nor holds a grant on is not visible to them at all, whatever organization permission they hold.

owner.description: Who `owner_user_id` is, resolved server-side in the same batch as `connected_by_label` (one per page). Same audience as a toolbox's `owner`: present on a connection the caller does NOT own, absent on their own. On every branch that returns a connection — list, detail and the command responses, so a transfer names the new owner without a reload. `name`/`email` are absent for an owner who has left the organization ("Former member").

name.description: Display name, else the email.

avatar_url.description: The person's picture — the same one the console's user menu draws: their stored profile picture, else a Gravatar URL (`d=404`, 96px) derived server-side from their email (the address itself is not sent), else null. Draw initials when it is null or the image fails to load.

shares.description: Present only when the caller may see the ACL: owner or `edit` access. A `view`/`use` recipient is never told who else the connection is shared with. Absent (not empty) when the caller may not see it.

can_share.description: Whether the caller may share this connection — owner, `edit` access, or a team admin on a team-granted one. No `connection:manage` fallback. Computed server-side (CLAUDE.md's API-first rule); the console reads this rather than re-deriving it from `owner_user_id`/permissions.

can_manage.description: Present on every list and detail row. Whether the caller may edit this connection's own settings — owner, or `edit` access. No `connection:manage` fallback. Computed server-side; same `can_manage` name used by toolbox and connector for the identical capability.

can_transfer.description: Present on every list and detail row. Whether the caller may transfer or delete this connection — owner, full stop. No `connection:manage` fallback. Deliberately narrower than `can_manage`: an `edit` grant lets someone use and reconfigure a connection, never give it away or destroy it.

can_revoke_share.description: `can_share`, verbatim — a THIRD formula, deliberately not an alias for `can_manage`: an `edit` grantee whose role omits `connection:share` (Auditor, Guest, any custom role) can reconfigure or reconnect the connection but was never meant to grant or revoke someone else's access to it, so `can_manage: true` on that row must not imply this control too. Mirrors `DELETE /connection/{id}/share/{aclId}`'s own gate exactly. Present on every list and detail row.

total.description: Every grant, the org-wide one included.

preview.description: At most 5 grantees, broadest first (org, then teams, then members), for a hover preview.

name.description: Display name; null for org grants and for grantees no longer in the org.

access_summary.description: Present only when `can_share` is true. Bounded by design — page `GET /connection/{id}/share` for the grants themselves.

access_via.description: How the CALLER reaches this connection — not who else can. `owner` — they own it. `direct` — a grant naming them personally. `team` — a grant to a team they belong to (or, per §6.2, one they administer), named in `access_via_team`. `org` — an organization-wide grant. When several sources apply the BROADEST wins and the caller's access level is not consulted: owner, else `org`, else `team`, else `direct`. So a caller granted `edit` personally AND `view` org-wide reads `org` — a narrower grant must never mask org-wide exposure, since this field says how far the connection reaches, not what the caller may do with it. Deliberately NOT gated on `can_see_shares`, and deliberately not a widening of it: this is the caller's OWN grant and their OWN team memberships, so a `view`/`use` grantee receives it while the grantee list — information about colleagues — stays closed to them. No other member is ever named. ABSENT when nothing reaches the caller — a transfer answering the ex-owner of a resource that was never shared, or a catalog row browsed with no grant behind it. Absent means "no source to name", never "not permitted", and never an implied `org`.

access_via_team.description: Present exactly when `access_via` is `team`, absent otherwise. The team the caller reaches this connection through — one of their own teams, never a disclosure about anybody else.

name.description: Team display name, or null when the team no longer resolves in the directory — the same null contract every resolved grantee name carries.

get.description: Status is reconciled against the vault on read. Connections the caller cannot see answer 404, never 403 — including another member's private connection, which no organization permission reaches. Resolves docs/access-model.md §4 ONLY, with no opt-in of any kind: the caller owns the connection, or holds a grant on it (directly, through a team, or org-wide). No grant, no fallback, `404` — even for a holder of `connection:manage`. There is no oversight read for connections; a `visibility` query parameter is not accepted. `can_share`, `can_manage` and `can_transfer` report whether the caller may share, edit or transfer/delete this connection, respectively — see the schema for each; none of the three has a `connection:manage` fallback any more (removed 2026-09-04) — ownership or a real grant are the only ways to reach them. `access_summary`, a bounded "who has access" rollup, is present only when `can_share` is true — page `GET /connection/{id}/share` for the grants themselves.

slug.description: The upstream connector the restriction is inherited from. For API consumers; never render it. Null — together with `label` — when the caller may not be told the upstream (an org-owned upstream they hold no grant on, or one that was deleted): a slug names the connector as surely as its label does.

label.description: The upstream's display name — null, together with `slug`, when the caller may not be told it. The UI then says "a connector this was forked from".

restricted_inherited_from.description: Set when this connector is restricted for the caller ONLY because the connector it was forked from is — a fork inherits its upstream's restrictions on purpose (forking a blocked connector is not a bypass), but nothing was set on the fork itself, so this says where the block came from. Null when not restricted, when a rule names this connector directly, or when the lineage could not be walked. Asking for access still targets THIS connector: approving the fork's own request lifts the inherited block for that fork only. Sibling of `restricted_by` (which stays the precedence layer); computed server-side in the same batch as the restriction evaluation — clients must not derive it from lineage.

connector_slug.description: Which connector this account is on.

owner_user_id.description: Owning member (`usr_…`); calls run as this identity. Owner is implicit `edit`, plus delete and transfer — the two things no share confers. Move it with `POST /connection/{id}/transfer`. This is who is ACCOUNTABLE for the connection now, which after a transfer is not who authenticated it — see `connected_by_user_id`.

connected_by_user_id.description: Who AUTHENTICATED this account (`usr_…`) — the member whose third-party credential the vault actually holds. Written once at creation and never rewritten. Distinct from `owner_user_id` on purpose: `POST /connection/{id}/transfer` moves the owner and deliberately does NOT touch the vault account, so after a transfer these are two different people and only this one may be rendered as "Connected by". **Null means NOT RECORDED, never "nobody"** — every connection created before this field existed is null, because nothing server-side could tell a never-transferred row (where `owner_user_id` would have been the honest answer) from a transferred one, and a fabricated attribution is worse than an absent one. Render nothing for a null.

connected_by_label.description: Display name for `connected_by_user_id`, resolved server-side one batch per page (name, else email). Present on every branch that returns a connection, commands included. A null HERE beside a NON-null `connected_by_user_id` is a fact about the person, not a failed lookup: they have left the organization, and clients render "Former member" — the same word the `GET /audit-log` actor summary uses. Compare the two fields, never one alone: a null id means "not recorded", a null label means "departed".
